blindSummary:
This state/province replicates a checkpoint script seen in a neighbouring state/province: district police arrested a foreign transgender person on suspicion of infiltration into the country, treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity. The state/province shares a long border with the same neighbouring country and falls within the same policing logic. It is also one of only three sub-national units recording cases in 2021 under the country's transgender-persons statute (3 of 7 nationally), indicating some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime is occurring at a detectable rate.

Local risk sits somewhat below the country-wide average. The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than the triple-sweep pattern documented next door. Compared with that neighbouring state/province, the harm here is a single documented arrest plus a broader infiltration framing rather than repeated mass operations; compared with the national capital territory, which shares the profiling language but also has the country's strongest institutional trans presence, this state/province lacks that offsetting civic infrastructure outside its largest city.

A welfare board exists (one of 12 sub-national units with a constituted body), but per an information-disclosure investigation it operates without a functioning policy framework. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism documented in the neighbouring state/province.
